1:
The five days are counted from different starting points, and nobody pretends the question is settled. Barnes takes them as the twelfth day after Paul's arrival at Jerusalem, the interval being occupied in the accusers receiving their summons and making arrangements. Clarke reckons them from the apprehension at Jerusalem and sets out Calmet's day-by-day scheme — Paul seized as the seven days of his vow were nearly ended, that is at the close of the fifth day after his arrival; before the council on the sixth, at Caesarea on the seventh, and five days after that, the twelfth from his arrival, the priests came down. Ellicott thinks the interval just allowed time for messengers to go from Caesarea to Jerusalem and for the priests to make their arrangements and engage their advocate, though he allows that dating the five days from Paul's departure from Jerusalem agrees better on the whole with the reckoning of twelve days that Paul himself gives a few verses later. Gill counts them from the coming to Caesarea rather than from the seizure in the temple, and notes that the Alexandrian copy reads after some days, leaving the number undetermined.

Who came down, and in what temper, is the more revealing question. Gill holds they came willingly and of their own accord rather than merely as accusers summoned by the chief captain, wishing to vindicate themselves lest they fall under the Roman governor's displeasure for encouraging tumults — the high priest being conscious he had acted illegally in ordering Paul to be smitten on the mouth in the midst of the council, and the elders knowing what a hand they had had in the conspiracy against his life. Henry marks the reversal of roles: those who had been his judges now appear as his prosecutors, and Ananias, who had sat to judge him, now stands to inform against him, disparaging himself and forgetting the dignity of his place; and Ananias is not ashamed to own himself a sworn enemy. The elders attended to signify their concurrence and to invigorate the prosecution, since no ordinary solicitor would follow it with the violence they desired; and the pains evil men take in an evil matter, Henry adds, should shame us out of our coldness in what is good. Calvin makes the journey itself an argument about the man's office — it was not meet for the highest priest to take such a journey, so that some other was highest priest at that time and Ananias was one of the chief priests, in great authority and an active man, who took the embassage upon himself. He notices the train of elders as calculated pomp, that the governor might be moved by the very sight of them; Wesley says only that Ananias would spare no trouble on the occasion.

The hired advocate draws the closest attention. Robertson observes that a Roman lawyer was necessary because the Jews were not familiar with Roman legal procedure, and that employing one was the custom in the provinces; the word for orator means a forensic advocate and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, the name being a diminutive of Tertius. Clarke thinks Tertullus was probably a Roman proselyte to Judaism, since he speaks everywhere as a Jew. Ellicott places such men in most of the provincial towns of the empire, ready to hold a brief for either side and bringing to bear their glib eloquence along with their knowledge of Roman law; and he demolishes the notion that the hearing was conducted in Latin. Proceedings before a procurator and his provincials were almost of necessity in Greek, as with our Lord and Pilate; Luke records when Paul spoke Hebrew and when Greek and would hardly have passed Latin over. Both he and Robertson add that the word rendered informed is a technical one, amounting to a formal indictment.
2:
Gill settles a smaller question first, that the one called forth was Paul and not the orator, as the Latin version puts beyond doubt by reading that Paul was cited, brought out of custody to hear the indictment. The flattery that follows is transparent, and the commentators spend most of their labour asking how much of it was true. Barnes allows that though the words were said in the customary style of orators, and though Felix was an unprincipled man, his administration really had produced much peace and order: he had taken a band of robbers under Eleazar and sent them to Rome, had arrested the Egyptian impostor who led four thousand into the wilderness, and had repressed the sedition between the people of Caesarea and the Syrians. Clarke names the same three services and turns them over: bad as the governor was, he had rendered these; but he is well known from his own historians and from Josephus to have been mercenary, oppressive and cruel, of all which the Jews brought proofs to Nero. Ellicott finds the administration offered little opening for panegyric beyond the suppression of the brigands, and admires the skill in the weight the orator lays on quietness. Robertson is harsher, since Tacitus also declares that Felix secretly encouraged the banditti and shared their plunder; but it sounded well to praise him for keeping a peace Tertullus was about to accuse Paul of disturbing.

Three of the words repay closer handling. Ellicott renders the phrase about worthy deeds as reforms or improvements; and on providence he observes that the Greek term then carried a higher sense than forethought, since the tendency to clothe emperors with quasi-divine attributes had put the providence of Caesar on their coins — Tertullus, after his manner, extending it to a procurator of Judaea. Robertson traces the same word and coins, and takes the other from its use for setting right broken limbs: Felix the reform governor of Judaea, he says, is a campaign speech, and it doubtless pleased its hearer. Barnes glosses the providence as foresight and vigilance, and cites Wetstein on the claim to accept it always and in all places: what we do in your presence, we do in your absence. Clarke puts it more shortly, that they talk of it not only before his face but behind his back.

What the speech is worth as pleading divides them. Clarke sets out its three parts, an exordium of praise, then the proposition, then narration and conclusion; he judges it artful enough though lame, and adds that its author had a very bad cause and that few with so bad a one could have made better of it. Wesley grants it nothing — a speech how different from Paul's, which is true, modest, solid and without paint, whereas this has a lame introduction, a lame transition and a lame conclusion; did not God confound the orator's language? Calvin objects not to complimenting a judge at all, but to this compliment, which is altogether corrupt, the rhetorician insinuating himself under false praises in order to darken the matter in question. To what end speak of peace and good order, except that Felix might think the safety of Judaea consisted in condemning Paul, and examine the matter no further? Josephus shows how covetously and cruelly the man behaved in that province, the murder of the high priest Jonathas being already past; so we see, Calvin says, how shamefully this orator lied, and how the accusers, blinded with hatred, cared nothing what befell their country so Paul might die. Ellicott catches the tact of the sycophant in the closing plea, where he speaks as though restraining himself from panegyrics his feelings would prompt, and marks the contrast the hired orator's epithet of clemency makes with the righteousness, temperance and judgment to come of which Paul afterwards spoke to this same ruler.
5:
The indictment opens with a noun, not an adjective, and every voice says the English has softened it. Barnes explains that Tertullus did not call Paul a pestilent fellow but the very pestilence itself, the word being the one applied to a plague and then to a man who corrupts others or excites tumult. Gill adds the forensic habit behind it, that Roman orators wishing to represent a man as dangerous to the state called him the pest of the city or of the empire, as may be seen in Cicero. Clarke, counting four particulars in the charge, matches the usage from Martial — thou art not a vicious man, Zoilus, but thou art vice itself — and follows Bishop Pearce in taking the next clause as stirring up tumults against all the Jews rather than among them, since otherwise the orator accuses his own countrymen of rising at Paul's instigation.

On the two charges that follow, the commentators divide between what a Roman court could hear and what it could not. Robertson observes that moving insurrections was an offence against Roman law if it could be proved, and quotes Furneaux's catalogue of what might have been alleged, from the plots at Damascus to the riot at Ephesus; specious proof could have been produced but was not, and the orator passed on to charges with which a Roman court had no concern. Ellicott takes the world to mean the empire, and notes a first occurrence in the name: this is the earliest appearance of the term of reproach transferred from the Master to the disciples. Barnes explains that the word rendered sect is the one from which heresy comes but properly means a party. Calvin wonders at the last count, since to be a Nazarite was rather a praise than a dispraise among the Jews. He supposes it to mean not the men lawfully consecrated to God but the assassins who gave themselves the specious name of zealots, though others, he allows, read it simply as Christians.

The temple charge and its sequel bring Lysias into the case. Clarke calls it a heavy accusation if it could have been substantiated, since the Romans let the Jews put to death anyone who profaned the temple, and traces it to the calumny about Trophimus the Ephesian, seen with Paul in the city and therefore alleged to have been brought inside; on the claim that they would have judged him by their own law he notes what actually happened, that had Lysias not interfered they would have murdered him on the spot Ellicott observes that the charge has been quietly modified, since what was once an assertion that Trophimus had been taken inside is now only an attempt, and that the advocate has turned the tumult into a legal arrest by temple officers. He adds that the words from according to our law to come unto thee are absent from many manuscripts, and if genuine are an attempt to make Lysias the real disturber of the peace. Robertson is certain they are a later addition, since they are missing from the chief uncials and contradict the earlier narrative, a clumsy attempt to complete a speech Luke had given only in summary. On the closing invitation they part company: Ellicott suspects a technical term, and that Tertullus was proposing the prisoner be examined by scourging or some other torture, keeping back the fact that he was a Roman; Robertson answers that torture was out of the question for a citizen, the word meaning no more than hearing what Paul had to say. Calvin finds the request fair on its face but reads the motive behind it: they had their witnesses ready and hoped that fine words would persuade Felix to hand over a man already condemned in their minds, false accusers always boasting that their matter is plain in order to blind the judge.
10:
Paul's bearing before he speaks is what the commentators notice first. Gill points out that he stayed silent under the charge until leave was given. Henry makes the silence deliberate: Paul let the orator finish according to the rules of decency and the method of courts, that a plaintiff be allowed to close his evidence before the defendant pleads; and when his turn came he made no reflection at all upon Tertullus, whom he knew to be speaking for his fee, but levelled his defence against those who had employed him. There are no flattering compliments in his opening, Henry adds, but the profession of a man who answers cheerfully because his own heart does not reproach him, and who does not stand trembling at the bar. Barnes adds that Paul founded his plea on the justice of his cause and would not by flattering words declare what was not strictly true; and Ellicott sets the apostle's frank manliness against the servile flattery of the advocate, noting that the verb rendered answer is the one behind our word apology in its older sense of vindication.

The compliment Paul does pay is a matter of arithmetic, and the commentators check it. Barnes explains that Felix had first governed Judaea jointly with Cumanus and took the province entire when Cumanus was condemned, so that about seven years had passed — long enough to have learnt the customs of the Jews, and long beside the tenure of his predecessors. Clarke calls it the sixth or seventh year, which may fairly be called many years when the frequent removals of provincial governors are considered, and glosses the word judge as answering to the Hebrew term for a ruler, the title of the ancient governors of Israel. Ellicott puts the figure at about six and defends the phrase on the same ground, that it exceeded the usual length of a procuratorship. Wesley disposes of it in a line: there was no flattery in this, it was a plain fact. Robertson agrees that Paul goes as far as he can in the way of a compliment, and no further, the governor having merely nodded to him to begin.

What Paul chose to argue, and what he left alone, is the last observation. Calvin notes that the defence does not argue the quality of the act but denies the crime outright — not because Paul was ashamed of the gospel or afraid of the cross, but because that was no place for a full confession of faith; so, omitting the cause of the gospel, which his accuser had never touched, he answers simply to the crimes charged. Calvin calls this a sincere and free manner of defending, to set matter against words, and meets an objection to the opening compliment: it is not that a long governorship could tell Felix when Paul arrived, but that a man long acquainted with the temper of the nation is likelier to deal moderately, since want of skill makes judges too credulous and hasty. Clarke sets out the plan — an exordium allowing the judge's competence, then refutation of the three charges and affirmation of three things: that he had kept a good conscience toward God and man, that so far from polluting the temple he had been purified in it, and that his accusers could produce no witness against him. Wesley finds the answer corresponding exactly to the three articles of the charge: against sedition, that he had not been long enough in the city to form a party; against heresy, that he confesses himself a Christian but holds the religion perfectly agreeable to the law and the prophets; and against profanation, that he had behaved in the temple peaceably. Henry adds the positive account, that Paul came up to worship God in peace and holiness and to keep up his communion with the Jews, not to affront them.
11:
The defence begins with a calendar. Barnes gives Beza's reckoning of the twelve days: one spent coming up to Jerusalem, one with James and the apostles, six in fulfilling the vow, the ninth the tumult and the rescue by Lysias, the tenth the council, the eleventh the plot and the removal to Caesarea — the days of confinement there not being counted, since nobody would pretend a man raised sedition from a prison. The point of the arithmetic is improbability: so short a space left no room for exciting a tumult. Clarke reads it the same way, that the time was quite insufficient to organise a sedition, and that not a single proof could be furnished of his having seduced any man by subtle disputation in the temple, the synagogues or the city, so that the charge fell self-confuted. Barnes notes that the vaguer accusation, of being a pest, was too general for Paul to trouble with. Robertson observes that Paul takes up the very word Tertullus had used for taking knowledge and repeats it back.

That word raises a question Calvin will not leave alone. Paul came for other causes, he says, and will presently confess the chief was to bring alms for the brethren; but he was not bound to give an account of his coming, and it remains true that he came with no other mind than to profess himself a worshipper of God. The harder question is how he can say he came to worship at all, when the religion of the temple was abolished and every distinction of place taken away. Calvin answers that Paul neither lies nor dissembles: the servants of Christ were not forbidden to worship in the temple, provided they did not tie holiness to the place but lifted up pure hands without choosing between places. It was lawful for him, being void of superstition, to use the solemn rites there, since he offered no propitiatory sacrifice contrary to the gospel; religion did not compel him to come up as the law had once required, yet he does not abhor an external worship which was to men a testimony of godliness. Barnes points out that the Greek is not quite what the English suggests — not that worship was his purpose in travelling, but that he was engaged in devotion when the tumult arose, his main design being to carry the benefactions of the Gentile churches. Ellicott takes the clause as the implied answer to the profanation charge: a man who had come to worship was not likely to be guilty of it.

The denial itself is flat and the challenge open. Gill observes that Paul was so far from moving sedition that he never so much as entered into conversation with anyone; he was indeed found in the temple, but purifying himself according to the law. Ellicott notes that the answer traverses every part of the indictment — not a discussion in the temple, not a crowd gathered anywhere in the city — and ends by demanding adequate evidence, two or three witnesses independent and agreeing. Robertson makes the same tally, that Paul denies the two serious charges and with them the only one a Roman court could entertain, and that the word rendered prove means to set a thing beside its claim: they have made assertions and not backed them. Calvin adds that Paul need not have denied any of it had he done it, since he might have answered that it was well done — he had been one of the scribes who disputed daily, Christ and the apostles had done the same, and he might have retorted the charge upon adversaries who did the same; but since his one aim is to show that importunate men had molested him for no cause, he treats not of the lawfulness of the fact but only of the fact.
14:
The one charge Paul admits he admits in his own words, and the wording is the point. Ellicott notes that the noun rendered heresy is the same the prosecutor used for sect and should have been translated alike, since as it stands the reader cannot see that the Way had been called a heresy at all; in choosing the term the Way, Paul adopts what the disciples used of themselves and protests by implication against a more invidious epithet. Barnes makes the same complaint of the English, which imports our idea of error in doctrine where the Greek says only party; and he notes what Paul does not stoop to answer, the contempt buried in the name Nazarenes. Robertson finds the confession frank and full: Paul is guilty of that and says so, but prefers his own word, claiming Christianity to be the whole and real Judaism rather than a sect of it, no deviation from it but its fulfilment. Wesley corrects the appellation on the same ground, not that the word was odious but that it was not honourable enough — a party is formed by men, whereas this way was prescribed by God; and Gill notes that Paul was never ashamed to own the truth, whatever the consequence.

Clarke asks why a neutral word was used to injure him, and answers from the politics of the council. The term carried no bad meaning among the Jews, the Pharisees themselves being called a sect, and Josephus, himself a Pharisee, speaking of the sect of the Pharisees. But two accredited parties already existed with their interests fairly balanced, both represented in the Sanhedrin, and the fear was that the Nazarenes would form a third and divide the influence of both — which is why the Christians had both for enemies. On the positive half of the answer Clarke has Paul bringing in no new object of worship and no new creed, and Barnes finds the appeal to the God of his fathers fitted to reach a Jewish hearer. Calvin weighs at length what Paul means by conceding the name. He thinks Paul means either that he is a Pharisee, as he had lately confessed, or that he calls the Jewish religion and the gospel that flowed from it a sect without reproach, both standing apart from the usage of every other nation. Calvin adds a caution against misusing the verse: the Papists are ridiculous who make Paul approve all manner of antiquity, for he never meant to ground religion in the authority of ancestors — a defence that would serve every Gentile superstition equally — but only to wipe off the blot of impiety cast on him.

The hope he professes next is chosen with an eye to the court. Barnes points out that the resurrection was held by the Pharisees present, so that in this cardinal point he maintained nothing they did not, and they could not arraign him for it. Ellicott sees the same tact as when Paul divided the council earlier, since he identifies himself not merely with the Pharisees but with the bulk of the nation. Calvin thinks the order deliberate: having first professed that he believes the Scripture, Paul then adds the hope of a resurrection, so that it may appear the hope comes neither from carnal sense nor from the decrees of men but is conceived out of the word of God, reverence for Scripture being the beginning of faith. On its reach the voices divide. Calvin presses the words about the just and the unjust against those who restrict the rising to the members of Christ, since by the plain voice of Christ all are cited, some to judgment and some to life. Robertson reports the opposite objection, that Luke misrepresents an apostle who held to no resurrection save for those in Christ, and rejects it as a mistaken reading.
16:
The conscience Paul claims is tied to the doctrine he has just confessed. Ellicott takes the herein to mean in this belief: because he held the resurrection as a stern reality, the one law of his life was to keep his conscience clear of wilful sin — words, he adds, almost as bitter to Felix as to Ananias, though the governor at least had the decency to listen in silence. Calvin makes the connection a general rule, that there is no sharper prick to drive men toward a godly life than the hope of the last resurrection, and turns it on those who lack it: an evil conscience is as good as a thousand witnesses to convict men of not believing an eternal life they never long after. He notes too that the word always signifies perseverance in a straight course, so that those truly hope for the resurrection who are never weary of well-doing. Wesley catches the edge in the sentence with two words, that Paul exercises himself as well as they.

The vocabulary interests Barnes and Robertson differently. Barnes takes the verb as making conscientiousness the leading habit of a life, and argues that a conscience void of offence requires two things, that it be rightly informed as to duty and that what is known to be right be honestly performed. Robertson notes that the same verb gives us the word ascetic, and that Paul claims to be at least the equal of his accusers in taking pains to please God. On the adjective he is more precise: the papyri use it to mean free from hurt or harm, and it can be read either actively, as not stumbling, or passively, as not stumbled against — the first fitting the clause about God and the second that about men. He adds Furneaux's remark that it must have been wormwood to Ananias to hear Paul repeat the very words for which he had once ordered him struck on the mouth. Clarke ties the verse back to the creed: because he believes in a resurrection of just and unjust and that every man shall be judged for the deeds done in the body, he exercises himself day and night — toward God in holding no opinion contrary to His truth, toward men in doing nothing he would not wish done to himself.

The last stroke of the defence is the errand itself. Barnes observes that a man who came to bring relief to a suffering people can hardly have come to defile their temple, the alms being the charities of the churches for the poor Christians of Judaea. Ellicott sets the interval at four years since the previous visit, which he thinks throws light on the earlier compliment about many years, and notes that this is the only mention in the whole book of the collection which fills so large a place in the letters of the period — an undesigned coincidence between history and epistles often dwelt on by writers on the evidences. Robertson reads the phrase as at an interval of several years rather than after many, and takes the offerings to be the sacrifices mentioned earlier for the four men and himself, without conceding that Paul had planned them before he came. Calvin makes the verse interpret the earlier one about worship, since Paul plainly did not travel in order to sacrifice but reports what the Jews found him doing; and he draws out two acquittals from it — the purifying witnesses that he did not pollute the temple, and the absence of any multitude leaves no ground for a charge of tumult. Clarke adds what the errand cost, the alms being the fruit of his own earning and influence among a foreign people. Gill reckons a longer reach still, some five and twenty years since his conversion, most of them spent among the Gentiles.
19:
The sentence breaks off, and the break is evidence. Robertson points out that the words about certain Jews from Asia have no verb: Paul seems to have meant to say that they charged him with these things, and instead stops to explain that they are not there — a thoroughly Pauline anacoluthon. He quotes Furneaux to the point: the accusers who were present had not witnessed the alleged offence, and those who could have given first-hand evidence were not present, so that there was no case in a Roman court. Barnes puts the consequence plainly: the only competent witnesses to what happened in the temple had stayed away, which showed they were not prepared to face examination, and the charge ought therefore to be dismissed. Ellicott supposes they shrank from the consequences of what they had begun and either stayed at Jerusalem or set out homeward when the feast was over. Wesley draws the wider moral: the world never commits greater blunders, even against its own laws, than when persecuting the children of God.

Having disposed of the absent, Paul turns to those present. Barnes calls it a bold appeal showing full consciousness of innocence, and observes that Paul grants their competence for the one occasion they had witnessed. Clarke sharpens the contrast: the Jews of Asia were the most competent witnesses, declared enemies though they were, and the men who had stirred up the persecution — why then are they kept back? Because they could prove nothing; let those who are here depose, if they found any evil in him when he was examined at Jerusalem. Robertson notes that the word for wrongdoing is chosen from the accusers' point of view, and adds Furneaux's remark that to a less sensitive conscience his conduct before the council would have seemed venial enough. Ellicott prefers the reading of the better manuscripts, what wrong act they found in me, and marks how narrow the ground has become: this was the single instance in which any words of Paul's had even been the occasion of an uproar, and what he then said was a belief he held with their best teachers, since before the council he had never reached the question of the Messiahship.

The one voice he owns has been read against him. Barnes reports the construction put on it by Chubb and other infidels, that Paul is confessing he was wrong to have cried out before the council about the resurrection, his conscience reproaching him for time-serving and for setting the two parties at odds on purpose. Barnes answers that Paul is doing nothing of the kind: he is fixing attention on the main thing he had said, which really was the chief doctrine he had been defending, and since that was the only matter these men had witnessed, he calls them to prove it wrong if they can. Gill reads it the same way, that Paul does not concede the voice to have been an evil in him, only that it was the one thing any of them — and a part of them only, the Sadducees — could judge evil. Clarke spells out the arithmetic: the Sadducees on the council may blame him for the belief, but the doctrine is credited by the nation at large, there is nothing criminal in holding it, and nothing else can be brought, so that this is the sum of all the charges he is called to answer. Calvin, taking the appeal as made to the council rather than to the governor's bench, draws the same inference from their silence at the time: they knew nothing then to lay to his charge, since they began to stir only at that one word, from which it appears that they now coin a new accusation for no cause — had there been any real fault in him, they would not have concealed it then.
22:
What the governor knew, and when, turns on how the verse is construed, and the translators are divided. Barnes lays out the two readings: one takes it that although Felix knew the doctrine better than Paul's accusers did, he nevertheless deferred the hearing until Lysias should come down; the other, which Barnes prefers with Beza, Grotius and Doddridge, makes the knowledge a thing still to be got — after I have been more accurately informed of this way, when Lysias has come down, I will hear the cause. He thinks the second confirmed by what follows, since Felix afterwards sent for Paul and heard him concerning the faith, evidently to inform himself. Clarke reaches the same conclusion by way of Wakefield's rendering and Calmet's, both putting the inquiry in the future, and for the same reason, that the private hearing came before Lysias was expected. Wesley takes it the same way and adds that Felix, being afterwards better informed, doubtless transmitted a full account to Rome. Robertson leaves the comparative open in another direction: Felix knew more accurately than the council supposed, though how he came by the knowledge is nowhere stated.

Where such a man could have learnt anything of the Way is answered alike by several. Ellicott points to Jerusalem, which a procurator would visit at the great festivals, and to Caesarea itself, where Philip the Evangelist had founded a community five and twenty years before that numbered Cornelius and other Roman soldiers; and Drusilla, being a Jewess, may have contributed something. Robertson adds a further possibility, that Felix knew of the ruling given at Corinth by Gallio, which treated Christianity as a form of Judaism. Henry supposes he had picked up at Caesarea the notion that the religion was not the evil thing it was represented to be, knowing some of that way to be honest men and very conscientious. Ellicott adds what the knowledge was worth in court: Felix was too well-informed to be moved by Tertullus, and could see that the prisoner was no common assassin or leader of sedition. Robertson says he knew perfectly well that the prosecution had failed; the pretext of needing Lysias in person was plausible and false, since Lysias had already declared Paul innocent in writing and was never summoned to Caesarea.

The adjournment itself is what the commentators condemn. Chrysostom reads the delay as management rather than caution: the long course of investigation meant it could not be said the trial was hurried, but Felix put them off on purpose, not because he wanted to learn, but because he wished to be rid of the Jews — on their account he did not like to release the prisoner, and to punish him was impossible, since that would have been too barefaced. The liberty afterwards allowed, and the leave given his acquaintance to minister to him, show that Felix too entirely acquitted him of the charges. Henry weighs the outcome both ways. It disappointed the priests that Paul was neither condemned nor remitted to their judgment, which he takes for an instance of God restraining the wrath of enemies by the agency of strangers rather than friends; but it was an injury to Paul that he was not released, since a judge who saw that nothing but malice lay behind the prosecution ought to have delivered him out of the hand of the wicked. It is a wrong not only to deny justice, Henry says, but to delay it — and this judge neither feared God nor regarded man. Ellicott finds the sequel worse, since the adjournment turned into an indefinite postponement — perhaps the accusers, having fired their last shot, judged the case lost and withdrew — and observes that detaining a prisoner so was a common incident of Roman provincial justice. Gill notes only that Felix heard what was said on both sides, as a judge ought.
23:
The terms of the custody are unusually easy, and every voice notices it. Gill states the bare position, that Paul was neither condemned nor acquitted and so had to be retained until one or other was done. Ellicott would render the officer as the centurion, either the one to whose charge Lysias had committed him or the one who had the care of prisoners awaiting trial, and finds the leniency a measure of the impression Paul had made: the clemency on which the orator had complimented Felix was not dead, but it was shown to the accused instead of the accusers. Clarke takes the liberty granted to mean release from the chains that bound him to his guards, and reads the phrase about his own people as covering his fellow Christians, free to bring him the conveniences of life and to visit as they pleased — ample proof that Felix found no evil in him, and he would have dismissed him outright but for two things, the wish to please Jews who could depose grievous matters against his administration, and the hope of money. Robertson glosses the word for indulgence as the opposite of strict confinement, though the man was still under guard, and notes that of these intimates we know the names of Luke, Aristarchus, Trophimus and Philip.

What the arrangement shows about the judge is read the same way by three of them. Barnes takes Felix to have regarded Paul as a persecuted man and the charges as malicious, and suspects the access allowed to friends was calculated, so that the prisoner might be furnished with means to purchase his freedom. Calvin argues from it that Felix, though he pronounced nothing, perceived Paul to be burdened with no fault of his own but with the malice of the priests. From the permission itself he draws another inference, that Paul's companions and the church had not forsaken him, since there would have been no point in granting access unless they were present and eager to serve him; and from their example we should learn not to defraud the martyrs of Christ of any comfort while they labour for the gospel. Wesley notes the effect of a prisoner at large: by this the gospel was spread more and more, not to the satisfaction of the Jews, though they could not hinder it.

The wife who came with him has a history the commentators tell in full. Barnes traces it from Josephus: daughter of the elder Herod Agrippa, betrothed to Epiphanes on condition that he embrace the Jewish religion and released when he refused, then given by her brother to Azizus king of Emesa, who consented to be circumcised; Felix saw her, fell in love, and sent Simon, a Cyprian Jew who passed for a magician, to persuade her away, and she was prevailed on to transgress the laws of her forefathers. She was therefore living in adultery, which Barnes thinks the reason Paul afterwards pressed chastity. Ellicott notes that she can scarcely have been ignorant of the new society, since she must have known of the death of James and the imprisonment of Peter, and may have connected her father's end in this very city with the part he had taken against the faith. Robertson sets the family record out starkly — her father murdered James, her great-uncle killed John the Baptist, her great-grandfather the children of Bethlehem — and suspects the phrase his own wife marks the occasion as no formal trial, Page holding that her curiosity procured the interview. Calvin allows that she had not quite abandoned the feeling of religion she had from a child, since Felix would hardly have desired to hear Paul but for his wife's sake; yet such revolts, he judges, are tickled with curiosity rather than moved by any sincere desire to learn.
25:
The three subjects were chosen for the two hearers. Barnes takes the first not as the righteousness God imputes but as justice in the relations of life — a fit opening, since dispensing justice was the man's office, and a judge who took bribes needed reminding of a Judge who cannot. The second word means not abstinence from drink but restraint of all the passions, and what Paul had in view was the adultery in which Felix was living. Gill reads the first the same way, not justifying righteousness but the doing of right between man and man, a virtue necessary in a judge and wanting in this one, whom the historian charges with much cruelty and injustice. Clarke matches each term to a vice: Felix was tyrannous, lived under the power of avarice, and had shown his incontinence in depriving the king of Emesa of his wife — while Drusilla, who had forsaken the husband of her youth for a bad man, deserved reprehension under the same heads.

That Paul chose them at all is what the commentators find remarkable. Barnes observes that his boldness is the more striking because he was dependent on this judge for his pardon: a timeserver would have flattered the man's vanity or palliated his vices, but the idea never seems to have occurred to Paul. Ellicott presses it further: it would have been easy to bring the pair over had the preacher been content to speak smooth things and put the patch of a ceremonial Judaism on the old garment of a sensual life; instead he pressed home what their state needed. Robertson says Paul turned the tables round, expounding the faith in Christ as it applied to his hearers: righteousness they did not possess, self-control they did not exhibit, a judgment certain to overtake them. Calvin marks the reversal of positions. Felix had hoped to take pleasure in the sermon, as men desirous of novelty feed their ears with subtle disputations, and to satisfy his wife's curiosity without trouble to himself; instead the prisoner disputes of the judgment of God, and the man who held power of life and death over him quakes as before his own judge, finding no comfort but to send the speaker away.

Why he trembled, and what it was worth, divides them. Clarke reports Bishop Pearce's explanation, that Felix feared not for himself but for his domestic peace, lest Drusilla, a Jewess who knew she had broken the law of Moses, should be moved by the discourse; and he answers it, since she is said to have turned heathen for her second husband's sake — so we may hope Felix felt real regret for his life, his conscience not being so seared as to keep out every gracious impression. Robertson notes that the conviction seems to have reached the governor only, since like another Herodias Drusilla's resentment was rather to be feared; she trusted, Wesley guesses, to her descent from Abraham or to the law's expiations. The promise of a convenient season Robertson reads as an excuse for dodging the personal turn the sermon had taken. Wesley draws the same conclusion with more grief in it: how happily might the conviction have ended had he pursued the views then opening on his mind, but like thousands he deferred them to a season that never came, and though he heard Paul again he was terrified no more. Calvin makes the general rule: the reprobate may be struck with the judgment of God and yet not be renewed to repentance by terror alone, since Felix, touched at hearing that God will judge the world, flees the judgment seat he fears — a feigned sorrow that does not work salvation. True repentance requires a fear that breeds a hatred of sin, and the token of real profiting is that a sinner seeks his medicine where he took his wound.
26:
Where the governor got the idea that there was money to be had is answered the same way by several. Ellicott says he had caught at the word alms in the defence: Paul was evidently not without resources, having either money of his own or wealthy friends, and something might be got out of one or the other for a freedom the prisoner would naturally desire. Gill reads the calculation the same way and adds what the prosecution had supplied, since the indictment presented Paul as the head of a large body of men and therefore a person whose liberty was valuable; the leave given his friends to visit and minister to him may itself, he suggests, have been granted with this in view. Robertson notes that Roman law required exile and confiscation of a magistrate who took bribes, but that the rule was lax in the provinces and Felix had doubtless taken them before, Josephus representing him as greedy for money. Calvin draws the inference from the prosecution's own eagerness: seeing the Jews sue so earnestly to have the man put to death, Felix scented that this was no common prisoner but one in great favour with many, and did not doubt that his friends would willingly bestow cost to redeem him — for such a ghoul, he adds, would not have been content with a small prey.

The wrong of it is what the commentators dwell on. Barnes points out that Paul had proved his innocence and should have been released at once, and that Felix instead kept him in custody hoping that a man wearied with confinement would buy his liberty. But Paul offered nothing: he knew what justice was, and would neither purchase what was already his due nor gratify a man who prostituted a high office for gain. Calvin observes that Felix, having thoroughly tried Paul's integrity, was ashamed to take money from the Jews for condemning him, and yet, being covetous, would not acquit him for nothing — which is how judges that gape after money insinuate themselves, making way for corruption by holding out fair words and some hope of deliverance. Clarke meets Bishop Pearce's question, how Luke could have known the governor's private motive, by pointing to Paul himself, with whom Felix held frequent conferences and to whom he undoubtedly expressed the wish. He adds a judgment on the man's origin, that Felix had been a freedman of Claudius and once a slave, and that the meanness of the slave was still apparent, made insufferable by a governor's authority.

The repeated interviews tell their own story. Ellicott finds it easy to imagine what passed in them — the suggestive hints, half promise and half threat, on the one side, and on the other the prisoner's steady refusal to buy what he claimed as a right, along with his fruitless attempts to work some change in his judge's character. Robertson catches the same persistence in the tenses, since Felix kept on hoping, kept on sending and kept on conversing, and was doomed to disappointment: he was never terrified again. Barnes finds that the strangest feature of all, that a man once so alarmed could hear the same speaker on the same subject unmoved; but the hope of money overcame it, and when sinners have once resisted the strivings of the Spirit they often sit unconcerned under the very truth that shook them. Calvin puts it as a verdict on the earlier trembling: it was plainly a vain and transitory fear, since the hope of gain now compels him to send for the man whom fear had compelled him to send away. Wesley calls it an evil hope, and no marvel that a man whose eye was not single profited nothing by all Paul's discourses — waiting for this, unhappy Felix fell short of the treasure of the gospel.
27:
The two years are counted from Paul's arrival at Caesarea, not from the beginning of the governorship. Gill makes that distinction, since Felix had been judge in the nation many years already. Robertson dwells on what the interval meant: Paul lingered in prison waiting for a second hearing that never came, and Caesarea became his compulsory headquarters for two years. He supposes Luke came and went with frequent visits to Philip the Evangelist, and thinks it probable that the material of the third Gospel was gathered in this period, and part or all of it written, the writer having ample opportunity to examine those who had heard Jesus. Ellicott is more cautious about filling the silence. Some have assigned the letter to the Hebrews to these years and others the letters to Ephesus, Colossae and Philemon, but he finds no adequate evidence for either; it is better to think of the apostle's patient resignation, learning obedience by the things he suffered, and of his intercourse with Philip and the church at Caesarea as a comfort to him. Robertson likewise dismisses those attempts as more specious than convincing.

Why the change of governor came when it did is answered from Josephus by nearly everyone. Robertson explains that during these two years Jews and Gentiles fought openly in the market-place at Caesarea, that Felix set the soldiers on the mob and many Jews were killed, and that a formal complaint to the emperor procured his recall. Ellicott gives the same cause and adds that the influence of his brother Pallas saved him from further punishment, while his successor, who reached the province about the year sixty, is described by Josephus as suppressing the brigands and keeping the country quiet. Barnes quotes the historian's own sentence — that when Festus was sent as successor, the principal inhabitants of Caesarea went up to Rome to accuse Felix, who would certainly have been punished had not Nero yielded to the solicitations of Pallas — and calls the agreement with Luke an undesigned coincidence, since Josephus never mentions Paul, yet establishes that Felix had every reason to court Jewish favour just then. Clarke tells the same story and Wesley the same in a line, that the accusations followed him to Rome and had utterly ruined him but for his brother's interest with Nero.

The last act is judged severely and unanimously. Robertson notes that the phrase for showing the Jews a pleasure is a banking figure, to place a favour on deposit, and that the deposit lodged was Paul in chains — adding that one manuscript gives a further motive, that Felix left him bound on Drusilla's account, she disliking Paul as much as Herodias disliked the Baptist. Ellicott renders the phrase the same way, to deposit a favour, and calls it an investment in iniquity, the boon conferred not being meant to go without return. Calvin observes that departing governors commonly released such prisoners as they knew to be innocent, and that Felix took the contrary course to win favour, making the guiltless servant of God a kind of offering for his own evil deeds in order to appease the priests. He infers something about Paul from the same fact: knowing that a judge who gaped for gain would have been favourable the moment money was offered, and having time enough to raise it, Paul plainly not only spared the brethren the cost but detested a bribery by which the holiness of civil order is shamefully polluted. Barnes and Clarke both draw the moral from the outcome, that the plan failed twice over — Felix sought money by injustice and got none, and sought the favour of the Jews by injustice and lost that too — so that honesty is the best policy, and, as Clarke puts it, like the dog in the fable he snatched at the shadow and lost the substance.
